title: Germany's flyover country takes its revenge
gist: The AfD's 43.8 per cent win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 September 2026 - three seats short of an absolute majority, against a CDU that collapsed to 17.2 per cent - is traced by Oliver Moody to 30 years of depopulation (a quarter of the state's population gone since 1990), industrial collapse and 'biographical erasure' rather than to campaign dynamics. Record 77.8 per cent turnout shows the AfD mobilised previous non-voters, and the party achieved this while openly radicalising rather than normalising.

insights.claim: In the Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 September 2026 the AfD took 43.8 per cent of the vote and 39 of 83 seats - three short of an absolute majority - while the CDU slumped to 17.2 per cent.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: A German state is now within three seats of outright radical-right government, a material step-change in the political risk premium attached to German domestic stability.
insights.quote: the radical right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party took 43.8 per cent of the vote and 39 of the 83 seats, three short of an absolute majority
insights.locator: At its state parliament election on 6 September

insights.claim: The AfD beat its own previous regional record - 32.5 per cent in Thuringia two years earlier - by more than 11 points, and more than halved conservative support in the same election.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: The trend is accelerating rather than plateauing; extrapolating prior AfD ceilings has been consistently wrong.
insights.quote: It has trumped its previous record vote share at a regional election – the 32.5 per cent it won next door in Thuringia two years ago – by more than 11 points.
insights.locator: This time, the AfD has beaten the CDU to a pulp

insights.claim: Turnout hit 77.8 per cent, the highest on record for the state, indicating the AfD's gains came substantially from mobilising people who had previously given up voting rather than from switching existing voters.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Turnout-driven gains are harder for mainstream parties to reverse than switcher-driven ones; polls that model the existing electorate will keep understating the AfD.
insights.quote: helping to drive turnout up to 77.8 per cent, the highest level on record
insights.locator: That message, as much as anything else

insights.claim: Polls badly underestimated the 2021 Saxony-Anhalt result when over-60s turned out en masse to hand the CDU a 16-point win, a reminder that regional German polling in this state has had large, non-directional errors.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Both tails are live: German state polling here has missed by double digits in each direction within five years.
insights.quote: They were utterly wrong: on the day itself, the over-60s turned out en masse to hand a stonking 16-point victory to the CDU
insights.locator: Five years later, the pollsters suggested

insights.claim: Unlike France's National Rally or the Sweden Democrats, the AfD has never undergone cosmetic normalisation and has instead gone through several cycles of compound radicalisation - meaning the usual European model of populist-right moderation-in-exchange-for-power does not apply.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Assumptions that the AfD will mellow as it nears power are unsupported by its trajectory; policy risk scales with vote share rather than being defused by it.
insights.quote: It has never really been through a process of cosmetic ‘normalisation’, like the dédiabolisation of the National Rally in France or the purging of neo-Nazi elements from the Sweden Democrats.
insights.locator: The AfD, which was founded in 2013

insights.claim: The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt manifesto pledged to segregate disabled children and refugees from schools, imprison teenagers for the mildest crimes and set up citizens' militias to watch over migrants - and it won 43.8 per cent on that platform.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Explicit extremism was not an electoral penalty in this contest, removing a constraint mainstream parties had relied on.
insights.quote: with pledges to segregate disabled children and refugees from schools, imprison teenagers for even the mildest of crimes, and set up citizens’ militias to help the police keep watch over migrants
insights.locator: The manifesto it put forward in Saxony-Anhalt

insights.claim: The AfD won despite abundant local evidence of extremism in its ranks, including a state leader who appeared to display a Hitler salute and senior staff who organised camps for a successor to the Hitler Youth.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Scandal-based containment strategies against the AfD have stopped working; expect mainstream parties to face pressure toward cooperation instead.
insights.locator: It has done so despite abundant local evidence

insights.claim: Saxony-Anhalt's unemployment peaked at 25 per cent after reunification as its chemicals, coal-mining and heavy machinery sectors were cut to the bone, and it remains a couple of points above the east German average.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Decades-old deindustrialisation shocks are still producing political outcomes; a useful base rate when assessing today's German industrial-job losses.
insights.quote: the unemployment rate peaked at 25 per cent and stayed sticky well into the 2000s
insights.locator: Even in comparison to other parts

insights.claim: Saxony-Anhalt's GDP per capita has more than doubled in real terms since reunification yet remains conspicuously behind neighbouring Saxony and Brandenburg, and it contracted 0.2 per cent last year - relative decline, not absolute, is what drives the vote.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Absolute income gains do not neutralise political revolt where peer comparison is unfavourable - a warning against using aggregate growth data to forecast political stability.
insights.quote: Saxony-Anhalt is doing a lot better than it was, but not as well as its peers.
insights.locator: Its GDP per capita has more than doubled

insights.claim: Saxony-Anhalt has lost a quarter of its population since 1990, a far higher proportion than any other German region, with the Wolfen-Nord estate falling from 35,000 residents to 6,000.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Depopulation of this magnitude destroys the local institutional fabric that mainstream parties depend on, leaving political space that a disciplined insurgent can occupy cheaply.
insights.quote: it has lost a quarter of its people since 1990, a far higher proportion than any other region of Germany
insights.locator: More importantly, it has lost a quarter of its people

insights.claim: The Mansfeld-Suedharz district lost more than 40 per cent of its population after copper mines operating since the Bronze Age were shut, and now has a median age of 50.6 years, among the highest anywhere in Europe.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Extreme local ageing plus mine closure is a reproducible profile for identifying the next politically volatile European regions.
insights.quote: the area now has one of the highest median ages found anywhere in Europe, at 50.6 years
insights.locator: A few miles to the west, the copper mines

themes.theme: Identity, grievance and the organisational ground game

insights.claim: 73 per cent of Saxony-Anhalt's electorate think east Germans are still in many respects second-class citizens, only 47 per cent say reunification was overall a success, and 43 per cent agree the AfD lets east Germans be proud of their achievements again.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Thirty-six years after reunification a majority of an east German electorate rejects the legitimacy of the settlement - a structural, not cyclical, driver of German political risk.
insights.quote: The polls showed that 73 per cent of the state’s electorate thought east Germans were ‘still in many respects second-class citizens’.
insights.locator: The polls showed that 73 per cent

insights.claim: The word 'identity' appears 33 times in the AfD's state manifesto, which proposes 'healing' a German identity hollowed out by guilt and multiculturalism by focusing schools and museums on a supposed golden age from 1871 to 1933.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: The AfD's programme is explicitly cultural-institutional, not just migration-focused; a governing AfD would target education and cultural institutions first.
insights.quote: The word ‘identity’ appears 33 times in the AfD’s state manifesto.

insights.claim: The AfD has woven itself into rural local life - dependably showing up to village barbecues and volunteer fire brigade fundraisers - while rival parties have unusually shallow roots in the state, giving it an organisational moat that polling does not capture.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Ground-game embeddedness, not messaging, is the durable asset here; it makes the AfD's vote share sticky even if national conditions improve.
insights.quote: Unlike its rivals, it dependably shows up to village barbecues and fundraisers for the volunteer fire brigade.
insights.locator: The other political parties have put down unusually shallow roots

insights.claim: Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his Berlin coalition carry favourability ratings between 10 and 15 per cent - comparable to insect burgers and the total abolition of cash - which functioned as a direct gift to the AfD's state campaign.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Federal unpopularity at this level makes further CDU losses in coming state elections the base case and raises the odds of leadership challenges in Berlin.
insights.quote: Merz and his ruling coalition in Berlin have roughly the same favourability ratings as insect burgers, AI managers in the workplace and the total abolition of cash (all between 10 and 15 per cent)
insights.locator: Siegmund had the even greater stroke of luck

insights.claim: In April 1932 the free state of Anhalt, fragmented and devastated by the Great Depression, gave the Nazis 41 per cent on a platform of national renewal and culture war; local conservatives then folded and helped install the party's first chief minister, nine months before Hitler seized absolute power.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: The watchpoint is not the AfD's vote share but whether the CDU breaks its cordon and enters coalition - historically that was the decisive step.
insights.quote: The Nazis, promising national renewal and a culture war against ‘decadent’ and Marxist elites, won 41 per cent of the vote. Ultimately, the local conservatives folded and helped Hitler to appoint his party’s first chief minister.
insights.locator: In April 1932 the free state of Anhalt

insights.claim: The author holds that AfD-Nazi parallels generally obscure more than they illuminate, while still arguing that the specific 1932 Anhalt coalition dynamic is worth bearing in mind - a deliberately narrow historical claim.
insights.speaker: Oliver Moody
insights.so_what: Calibrates the analogy: the risk to watch is elite accommodation under electoral pressure, not a literal repeat.
insights.quote: History is clearly not about to repeat itself with any great precision. But it is worth bearing in mind.
insights.locator: History is clearly not about to repeat itself
